title: Quadratics
summary:
A **quadratic** is an equation where the highest power of the unknown is **2**, written in standard form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$. Its graph is a parabola, and it can have **two, one, or no** real solutions — which is itself useful information (it tells you, for instance, whether a projectile reaches a height or a process has a feasible operating point).

**Method 1 — square roots**, when there's no $bx$ term. If $ax^2 = k$, just isolate $x^2$ and take the root: $2x^2 - 8 = 0 \Rightarrow x^2 = 4 \Rightarrow x = \pm 2$. Remember the $\pm$: every positive number has two square roots. (For a physical quantity you usually keep the meaningful one.)

**Method 2 — factoring**, the quickest route when the numbers are friendly. Write the quadratic as a product of two brackets that multiply back to it, then use the fact that **if a product is zero, one of the factors must be zero**. For $x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0$, find two numbers that multiply to $+6$ and add to $+5$ (that's $+2$ and $+3$): $(x+2)(x+3) = 0$, so $x = -2$ or $x = -3$. The roots are where the parabola crosses the $x$-axis.

**Method 3 — the quadratic formula**, which *always* works, even when factoring won't: $$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.$$ Read $a, b, c$ straight off the standard form and substitute carefully (mind the signs). For $2x^2 + 3x - 2 = 0$: $a=2, b=3, c=-2$, so $x = \dfrac{-3 \pm \sqrt{9 + 16}}{4} = \dfrac{-3 \pm 5}{4}$, giving $x = \tfrac12$ or $x = -2$.

**The discriminant**, $b^2 - 4ac$, is the part under the root and it tells you the *number* of real solutions before you finish: positive ⇒ **two** real roots, zero ⇒ **one** (repeated) root, negative ⇒ **no** real roots (the parabola misses the axis). Checking the discriminant first can save you work — and tells you something physical about whether a solution exists at all.

Strategy: get it into $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ first; if there's no $bx$ term use roots; try quick factoring; otherwise reach for the formula. Always expect up to two answers, and decide which are physically meaningful.

equations.name: Standard form & solve by roots
equations.useWhen: There is no middle ($bx$) term. Isolate $x^2$, then take the square root of both sides — and keep the $\pm$.
equations.note: Every positive number has two square roots; choose the physically meaningful sign for real quantities.

equations.name: Factoring (zero-product rule)
equations.useWhen: The quadratic factors nicely. Find two numbers that multiply to $c$ and add to $b$; set each bracket to zero (a product is zero only if a factor is).
equations.note: The roots are where the parabola crosses the $x$-axis. Quick when $a=1$ and the numbers are tidy.

equations.name: Quadratic formula
equations.useWhen: Always works — especially when factoring isn't obvious. Read $a,b,c$ from $ax^2+bx+c=0$ and substitute carefully, watching signs.
equations.note: The $\pm$ gives the two roots. Compute the discriminant $b^2-4ac$ first to know how many real roots to expect.

equations.name: Discriminant (how many roots)
equations.useWhen: Checking, before solving, whether real solutions exist. The sign of $b^2-4ac$ tells you two / one / none.
equations.note: A negative discriminant means the parabola never crosses the $x$-axis — no real solution (physically, the target isn't reached).

glossary.definition: An equation whose highest power of the unknown is 2, in standard form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ with $a \neq 0$. Its graph is a parabola.
$ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ — get the quadratic into this shape first so you can read off $a$, $b$, $c$ for factoring or the formula.
A value of $x$ that satisfies the equation; graphically, where the parabola crosses the $x$-axis. A quadratic has up to two.
Writing the quadratic as a product of two brackets, e.g. $(x+2)(x+3)$. Then the zero-product rule gives the roots directly.
If a product equals zero, at least one factor is zero. So $(x+p)(x+q)=0$ means $x=-p$ or $x=-q$.
$x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ — solves any quadratic from its coefficients, whether or not it factors.
$b^2 - 4ac$, the part under the root. Positive ⇒ two real roots, zero ⇒ one, negative ⇒ none.
The U-shaped graph of a quadratic. It opens upward if $a>0$, downward if $a<0$; the roots are its $x$-axis crossings.

tips: **Get to standard form first.** Move everything to one side as $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ before reading off $a$, $b$, $c$ — sign mistakes here ruin the formula.
**No middle term ⇒ use roots.** If there's no $bx$, isolate $x^2$ and square-root both sides. Keep the $\pm$ — there are two roots.
**Try factoring when numbers are tidy:** two values multiplying to $c$ and adding to $b$. If you can't spot them quickly, switch to the formula.
**The formula never fails.** $x = \frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ works for every quadratic. Substitute with brackets to keep negative signs correct.
**Check the discriminant first.** $b^2 - 4ac$ tells you two / one / no real roots before you commit — and flags when no real solution exists.
**Expect two answers, then choose.** Decide which root is physically meaningful (a length, time or mass can't be negative).
